item.text: {"text":"Recent work supports modeling complementarity separately from semantic similarity. [Revisiting Graph Projections (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09209) infers complementary recommendations using a directed, weighted item graph projected from historical user–item interactions, offering a simple interaction-only starting point without pretrained language weights. [SComGNN (AAAI 2024)](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/28734) models complementary products through both relevance and dissimilarity: low-pass and mid-pass graph filters capture these components, with attention combining them. These results motivate retaining directional transition evidence rather than relying entirely on embedding similarity; neither establishes that arbitrary consecutive purchases are true complements.\n\nFor the constrained benchmark, a reasonable synthesis—not a verified published recipe—is a SASRec residual combining smoothed directed transition scores with separate source/target item embeddings and a title/description encoder trained from scratch using token embeddings plus pooling or a small CNN. Text can share statistical strength across sparse items, while asymmetric interaction scores learn which related items tend to follow others. Compare transition-only, text-only, and combined variants using macro validation HR@10 across all four categories. Treat graph edges as predictive associations, not compatibility labels; semantic similarity does not establish substitution, and purchase order does not prove a satisfied need. The search did not identify a verified 2024–2026 method satisfying every restriction simultaneously. [STAR (CIKM 2024)](https://pure.uva.nl/ws/files/245900224/3627673.3679999.pdf) is relevant text-recommendation work, but its transformer-based representations and review inputs make it unsuitable as a direct match."}
